extracted.intended_audience: readers of theological and political philosophy (clergy, magistrates, educated lay readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and interpretive standards for Scripture concerning eternal life, hell, the Kingdom of God, redemption, and the definition/authority of the Church in a commonwealth. Includes theological and political consequences (sovereign authority over public religion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternal life reckoned from Absolution, not Resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is reckoned from the Absolution, not from the Resurrection of them that are elected in Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the faithful may die and remain dead until the Resurrection, Eternal Life is understood as granted by Christ's absolution (i.e., by being 'written in the Book of Life') rather than commencing only at bodily resurrection. (Quotes/argument: comparison with Adam's loss of eternal life and the faithful's recovery through Christ.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of Heaven denotes the people ruled by God (not necessarily an ascent to empyreal Heaven)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Kingdom of Heaven is meant the Kingdom of the King that dwelleth in Heaven; his Kingdom was the people of Israel, whom he ruled by prophets and vicars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'Kingdom of Heaven' can indicate the community under God's rule (historically Israel, and later the Church), not necessarily that the faithful ascend to a literal higher Heaven above the stars. The author cautions against inferring a physical ascent of all saints into a special empyrean region absent Scripture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Souls of departed may be with God before bodily resurrection; immortality of man is by resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: Though bodies do not ascend until the general day of Judgment, souls appear to be with God after departure; the Resurrection proves the immortality of the whole man rather than proving an inherent, independent immortality of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passages (e.g., Luke 20, citations of patriarchs) can be read to show souls 'live to God' after death; however, Scripture does not plainly assert the soul's natural, independent immortality — immortality of man is effected by God's promise and the Resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality of the soul is not plain in Scripture; resurrection is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that the soul is naturally eternal and independent of the body is not apparent in Scripture; the immortality of man is by the Resurrection at the last day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Job 14 and St. Peter's epistles are cited to argue that immortality in Scripture is promised for the resurrection era, not as an intrinsic property of human nature except by divine grant (with few exceptions like Enos and Elias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God as a civil commonwealth located on Earth
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdom of God is a civil common-wealth where God reigns (by virtue of covenant) through a vicar or lieutenant; after Christ's coming again the Kingdom is to be on Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive and political claim: Scriptural passages are read to mean that when Christ returns to reign, God's Kingdom will be an earthly, societal order (Jerusalem as seat) rather than an otherworldly removal of the faithful to a higher Heaven. This connects theological salvation to political order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural depictions of Hell are metaphorical regarding place and mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Hell (Infernus/Hades under ground, Tartarus, Lake of Fire, Utter Darkness, Gehenna) are not to be taken as indicating specific literal geography but use metaphor derived from past judgments and images (e.g., Sodom's fire, Gehenna's burning refuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because literal readings (infinite-bottom pits, etc.) conflict with cosmological proportion and scriptural context, these images should be interpreted to convey general conditions (destruction, shame, exclusion) rather than precise physical locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satan, Devil, Abbadon are appellatives (offices), not proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Names like The Enemy, the Accuser (Diabolus), The Destroyer (Abbadon) set forth an office or quality rather than an individual proper name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terms function as descriptors of the enemy of God's people (often earthly opponents of the Church) and should not be rendered as personal names in translation; misreading them as proper names promotes superstition about devils as individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torments of Hell are metaphorical of moral/psychological and political suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Torments described as 'weeping and gnashing of teeth', 'the worm of conscience', fire, shame, and contempt signify grief, discontent of mind, and bodily calamities analogous to living under evil rulers and having God as enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metaphors communicate the pain of losing eternal felicity by one's own unbelief and disobedience. 'Everlasting fire' and 'unquenchable' indicate enduring destruction/torture until death (a 'Second Death'), not necessarily an eternal, undying conscious existence of individuals in torment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvation equals remission of sins and deliverance from death/misery
rubrics_metrics.description: The joys of Life Eternal are comprehended under 'SALVATION' — remission of sins and salvation from death and misery are the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because sin brought death and misery, to be saved from sin is logically to be saved from its consequences. Scriptural examples (e.g., healing of the palsied man where Jesus says 'thy sins be forgiven thee') are used to show equivalence between forgiveness and restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of general salvation is Jerusalem/Earth; 'Salvation is of the Jews'
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual evidence (Isaiah, Joel, John) indicates that the chief seat of God's Kingdom and the source of general Salvation will be Jerusalem on Earth, and that salvation 'begins at the Jews.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic and Gospel passages are read to support an earthly, Jerusalem-centered consummation from which salvation proceeds to the Gentiles; 'Salvation is of the Jews' is interpreted historically/linearly rather than spatially otherworldly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption presupposes a ransom/oblation accepted by God, not a compensatory satisfaction equivalent to the offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Salvation of a sinner supposes a precedent redemption (ransom), but that ransom is not a satisfaction for sin equivalent to the offense; rather, it is an oblation God is pleased to accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human attempts at recompense cannot cancel sin as a vendible thing; in Scripture God accepted sacrifices and oblations. Christ's death is described as the oblation demanded by God to enable salvation of repentant believers — not a transactional equivalence but a divinely accepted price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church (ecclesia) has multiple scriptural senses (house, assembly, universal, elect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'Church' signifies (1) God's House/temple, (2) a congregation or assembly, (3) the whole multitude of Christian men dispersed, (4) certain parts of Christians, or (5) the Elect/Church Triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context determines sense: references to silence in 'the Churches' may mean assembled congregations; 'Christ is Head of the Church' may mean all professing Christians; 'a glorious Church' refers to the elect. Translators and interpreters must attend to these distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: A Church can be 'one person' only as an assembly under lawful sovereign authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Only when taken for a lawfully constituted assembled congregation (i.e., under one sovereign authority) can the Church be said to have corporate powers (will, pronounce, command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without lawful warrant from the civil sovereign an assembly's acts are not the corporate acts of a Church but merely the acts of individuals present. The author defines a Church as 'A company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign; at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful Church (ecclesia legitima) requires summons by lawful authority; unlawful assemblies are concourses
rubrics_metrics.description: When assemblies are called forth by lawful authority they are 'Ecclesia Legitima'; when excited by tumultuous or seditious clamor they are 'Ecclesia Sugkechumene' (a confused/unlawful Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public assemblies for worship or decision-making require civil sanction; gatherings without such warrant are not to be regarded as lawful corporate Churches with authority to bind the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal earthly Church; Church capable of commanding coincides with the civil commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no universal Church on Earth that all Christians are bound to obey because no single earthly power rules all states; a Church capable of commanding is effectively a civil commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal and spiritual government are not distinct in legal effect: the civil sovereign, as chief pastor, holds the office necessary to prevent faction and contradictory doctrines. This grounds the political argument that religion's public aspects fall under sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign as sole interpreter and judge of divine commands in the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: As Abraham alone had authority to receive and interpret God's commands for his household, so the sovereign in a commonwealth is the only interpreter of what God has spoken for that polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because God spoke to Abraham and not to all members directly, positive commands for public religion should be received through the sovereign; this entails that those without supernatural revelation must obey the sovereign's laws concerning external religious acts, while inward belief remains beyond civil jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private revelation contrary to sovereign's law may be punished; inward belief is exempt
rubrics_metrics.description: It was lawful for Abraham to punish subjects who pretended private visions to oppose his religion; similarly, a sovereign may punish private spirits that oppose the public religion, but cannot legislate inward thoughts and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between external acts (subject to sovereign law) and inward thought (known only to God). The sovereign's power includes penalizing public dissent rooted in private revelation when it threatens the common order.
